'''''Pilea peperomioides''''' ({{IPAc-en|p|aɪ|ˈ|l|iː|ə|_|p|ɛ|p|ə|ˌ|r|oʊ|m|i|ˈ|ɔɪ|d|iː|z}}<ref>Interview of Dr {{ill|Phillip Cribb|nl|Phil Cribb}} by Jane Perrone on [http://www.janeperrone.com/on-the-ledge/2017/9/15/episode-seventeen-seeking-pilea-peperomioides-why-everyone-wants-the-chinese-money-plant Episode 17: Seeking ''Pilea peperomioides'' - why everyone wants the Chinese money plant] (01:40) of ''On the Ledge'' podcast. 15 September 2017. Retrieved 10 June 2018.</ref>), the '''Chinese money plant''',<ref>{{Inaturalist taxon}}</ref> '''UFO plant''', '''pancake plant, lefse plant''' or '''missionary plant''',<ref name="RHSPF">{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Pilea peperomioides''|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/13015/Pilea-peperomioides/Details|access-date=16 January 2021}}</ref> is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the nettle [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Urticaceae]], [[native plant|native]] to [[Yunnan]] and [[Sichuan]] provinces in [[southern China]].

[[File:Pilea peperomia and pups.jpg|thumb|alt=Pilea peperomioides and pups|Pilea peperomioides and its pups]]

==History==
The Scottish botanist [[George Forrest (botanist)|George Forrest]] was the first westerner to collect ''Pilea peperomioides'', in 1906 and again in 1910, in the [[Cang Mountain]] range in [[Yunnan|Yunnan Province]].

In 1945, the species was found by Norwegian missionary Agnar Espegren in Yunnan Province when he was fleeing from Hunan Province. He took [[cuttings (plant)|cuttings]] of ''P. peperomioides'' back to [[Norway]], by way of [[India]] in 1946, and from there it was spread throughout [[Scandinavia]].

''Pilea peperomioides'' is an example of a plant that has been spread amongst amateur gardeners via cuttings, without being well known to western botanists until the late 20th century. This led to the plant earning the nickname of "friendship plant", or "pass-along plant". Many horticulturists and hobbyists were not aware of its true classification, in the nettle family [[Urticaceae]], until the 1980s. The story of its identity and discovery in Western cultivation, along with its first published image, was detailed by Alan Radcliffe-Smith in 1984,<ref name="Radcliffe1">Radcliffe-Smith, A (1984) ''Pilea peperomioides'' (Urticaceae). ''Kew Magazine'' 1(1): 14–19</ref> and later in a more popular account by Phillip Cribb and Leonard Forman in 1987.<ref>{{cite web|title=A Chinese puzzle solved - ''Pilea peperomioides''|url=http://www.wildchicken.com/nature/garden/ga008_a_chinese_puzzle.htm|accessdate=30 June 2013|archive-date=9 August 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220809083125/http://wildchicken.com/nature/garden/ga008_a_chinese_puzzle.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>Cribb, P & Forman, L (1987) A Chinese puzzle solved. ''The Garden'' 112(12): 550–552</ref> Through the early 2010s and 2020s, ''P. peperomioides'' became widely available commercially, and is no longer a curiosity. The initial offerings for sale on the mainstream plant market saw great demand for the plant, with prices going as high as US$75 for a single unrooted cutting, advertised on [[Instagram]], as late as 2019.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.vox.com/the-goods/2019/3/21/18274568/pilea-peperomioides-plant-instagram-sill-circular-leaves |title=The Instagram-famous plant that used to be impossible to find |author=Ellen Airhart |publisher=Vox |date=21 March 2019 |accessdate=26 September 2022}}</ref>

==Description==
''Pilea peperomioides'' is an erect, [[evergreen]] [[perennial plant]], with shiny, dark green, circular leaves up to {{convert|10|cm|0|abbr=on}} in diameter on long [[petiole (botany)|petioles]].<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z Encyclopedia of Garden Plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1405332965|pages=1136}}</ref> The leaves are described as [[leaf shape|peltate]]—circular, with the petiole attached near the centre. The plant is completely hairless. It grows to around {{convert|30|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall and wide in the wild.  Indoors, it has the potential to grow larger. The stem is greenish to dark brown, usually unbranched and upright, and [[lignified]] at the base when mature. In poor growing conditions, it loses its leaves in the lower part of the stem and assumes a distinctive habit. The flowers are inconspicuous. The species is monoecious. Male flowers are more common, and female flowers may not be produced.<ref name="Radcliffe1"/>

The plant has a superficial resemblance to some species of ''[[Peperomia]]'' (hence the specific epithet ''peperomioides''), also popular as cultivated plants but in a different family, the [[Piperaceae]].  It is also sometimes confused with other peltate-leaved plants such as ''[[Tropaeolum majus|Nasturtium]]'', ''[[Umbilicus (plant)|Umbilicus]]'' and ''[[Hydrocotyle]]''.

==Range==
This species occurs only in China: in the southwest of [[Sichuan|Sichuan province]] and the west of [[Yunnan|Yunnan province]]. It grows on shady, damp rocks in forests at altitudes from {{cvt|1500|to|3000|m|ft|-2}}. It is endangered in its native habitat. However, it is kept in China and worldwide as an [[ornamental plant]].

==Cultivation==
In [[temperateness|temperate]] regions, ''P. peperomioides'' is treated as a [[houseplant]], with cultivation recommended at a minimum temperature anywhere from {{convert|13|C|F|abbr=on}}<ref>William Davidson. [https://books.google.com/books?id=XLITEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA110 "Chinese Money Plant."] ''Doctor Houseplant: An Indispensable Guide to Keeping Your Houseplants Happy and Healthy.'' Cool Springs Press, 2020. p. 110. {{ISBN|9780760369869}}</ref> to {{convert|5|C|F|abbr=on}}.<ref name="RHSPF"/> However, in its native range, the plant tolerates periods near or below freezing.<ref name="Perrone">Jane Perrone. ''Legends of the Leaf: Unearthing the secrets to help your plants thrive.'' Unbound, 2023. [https://books.google.com/books?id=OYOREAAAQBAJ&pg=PT208 n. pag.] {{ISBN|9781800182011}}</ref>  Thus the plant could be kept in unheated indoor areas or even outdoors in temperate climates; the foliage may be killed back by frost, but regrows in spring.<ref name="Perrone"/>  [[Wessel Marais]], the [[Kew Gardens]] botanist who [[#History|determined the identity]] of the plant in the 1980s, later grew the plant outdoors in [[Cazillac]], France.<ref name="Radcliffe2">Radcliffe-Smith, A (1997) A supplementary note on the cultivation of ''Pilea peperomioides''. ''Curtis's Botanical Magazine.'' 14(1): 55-56. {{doi|10.1111/1467-8748.00063}}</ref>  He reported it surviving for 6 or 7 years with temperatures as low as {{convert|-9|C|F|abbr=on}}, noting that "the stems above ground are killed but it comes again from below ground-level, so deep planting should do the trick".<ref name="Radcliffe2"/>

''P. peperomioides'' is propagated from plantlets that sprout on the trunk of the parent plant (these are called offshoots) or from underground shoots (called [[rhizome]]s).<ref name="Stanwyck">{{cite book |last1=Stanwyck |first1=Mary |title=The Pilea Peperomioides Handbook: An Illustrated Guide to Caring for Your Chinese Money Plant |date=2020 |publisher=Pilea Publications |location=London |pages=15–17}}</ref> These offshoots are often passed on as a lucky plant ("lucky thaler") or friendship plant. Since constant temperatures and high humidity have a positive effect on plant growth, this plant species is suitable for planting [[terrarium]]s.

Although the plant is endangered in its native habitat, it is among the most popular houseplants today. It is in high demand because it is slim, easy to grow, and tolerates dry environments. The plant is readily available in retail greenhouses, which in turn are supplied by industrial-scale farming enterprises.

This species has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name="RHSPF" /><ref>{{cite web|date=July 2017|title=AGM Plants - Ornamental|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf|accessdate=30 April 2018|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|page=78}}</ref>

There are three different cultivars which have appeared in the last few years 'Sugar', 'White Splash' and 'Mojito'.

== Propagation ==
''P. peperomioides'' is [[Plant propagation|propagated]] through divisions and stem cuttings.

Stem cuttings in ''Pilea peperomioides'' are often confused with leaf cuttings, as the propagation technique requires slicing off a leaf of the mother plant; however, the cutting must take place at the stem and include stem tissue for successful propagation. Hence it is technically a stem cutting not a leaf cutting.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.wikihow.com/Propagate-Pilea | title=How to Propagate Pilea: 3 Simple Methods }}</ref>
